competition: St. Petersburg Mathematical Olympiad, grade 9 (city round and selection round)

problems.problem: Two distinct quadratic trinomials $f(x)$ and $g(x)$ with leading coefficients equal to one are given. It is known that $f(19)+f(92)=g(19)+g(92)$. For which $x$ does the equality $f(x)=g(x)$ hold?

The following operation may be performed on a natural number $A$: split it into two natural summands greater than $1$ and replace $A$ by their product. Prove that from every number greater than $4$ an exact power of ten can be obtained by such operations.

All $120$ faces of twenty identical cubes with edge length $1$ were painted black and white, $60$ faces of each colour. Prove that the cubes can be placed on a table so that their bottom faces form the boundary border of a $6\times 6$ square, and among the faces that are visible the number of black ones equals the number of white ones.

Similar right triangles $ABC$ and $A'B'C'$ (the angles at the vertices $B$ and $B'$ are right; corresponding vertices are denoted by the same letters; the vertices are listed clockwise) are placed in the plane so that $A=C'$, and the point $A'$ lies on the ray $BC$ beyond the point $C$. Prove that the centre of the circle circumscribed about the triangle $A'AC$ lies on the line $A'B'$.

Numbers are placed in the cells of an $N\times N$ table so that at the intersection of the $i$-th column and the $j$-th row stands the number $1/(i+j-1)$. Then $N$ rooks were placed in the cells of the table so that no two rooks attack each other. Prove that the sum of the numbers under the rooks is at least one.
Inside the side $AB$ of a triangle $ABC$ there is a point $D$ such that $AD/DC=AB/BC$. Prove that the angle $ACB$ is obtuse.

Two ten-digit numbers $A$ and $B$ are given whose decimal representations contain only the digits $1$ and $2$. Prove that the number of twenty-digit numbers from which the number $A$ can be obtained by deleting digits equals the number of those from which the number $B$ can be obtained.

A point $D$ is taken inside the side $BC$ of an equilateral triangle $ABC$. The line passing through the point $C$ parallel to $AD$ meets the line $AB$ at a point $E$. Prove that $CE/CD\geqslant 2\sqrt3$.
Every second $54$ or $77$ is added to a natural number. Prove that after some time a number whose last two digits coincide will be obtained.

There are $nk$ stones, distributed somehow into $n$ piles. One may double any pile by moving into it, arbitrarily, stones from the other piles. For which $k$ can one always (for every $n$) achieve by such operations that all remaining piles contain equally many stones?
Prove that if a natural number $a$ is not a perfect square, then there is a natural number $n$ such that $a=[n+\sqrt n+1/2]$.
A regular $n$-gon $M$ was rotated about its centre through the angle $\pi/n$, giving an $n$-gon $M'$. Into what smallest number of convex polygons can the figure $M\cup M'$ be cut?
The sequence $(F_n)$ is defined as follows: $F_1=1$, $F_2=2$, $F_{n+2}=F_{n+1}+F_n$ for every $n>0$. Prove that for every natural $n$ the inequality $$\sqrt[n]{F_{n+1}}>1+1\big/\sqrt[n]{F_n}$$ holds.

The plane is coloured in $1992$ colours, and a triangle $T$ is given in it. Prove that there is a triangle in the plane congruent to $T$ such that on each pair of its sides there are interior points of the same colour.

$128$ ones are written on the board. In one move one may replace a pair of numbers $a$ and $b$ by the number $ab+1$. Let $A$ be the largest number that can be obtained on the board after $127$ such operations. What is its last digit?
Find all natural numbers that are powers of two and from which another power of two can be obtained by writing some digit in front.
A quadrilateral $ABCD$ is inscribed in a circle. The lines $AB$ and $CD$ meet at a point $M$, and the lines $BC$ and $AD$ at a point $N$. It is known that $BM=DN$. Prove that $CM=CN$.

Several people divide an inheritance they have received. Call an heir "poor" if he received less than $99$ roubles in the division, and "rich" if he received more than $10$ thousand roubles. It is known that in every division of the inheritance the amount of money of the "rich" heirs is not less than that of the "poor" ones. Prove that in every division of the inheritance the amount of money of the "rich" heirs is at least $100$ times that of the "poor" heirs.

Natural numbers $a$, $b$ and $c$ are such that $\dfrac{ab}{a-b}=c$. It is also known that the numbers $a$, $b$ and $c$ have no common natural divisor greater than $1$. Prove that $a-b$ is a perfect square.

Several points are given in the plane. One may replace a pair of given points $A$, $B$ by a pair of new points $C$, $D$ if the segments $AC$ and $BD$ have the same length, are perpendicular to $AB$, and the points $C$ and $D$ lie on different sides of the line $AB$. Prove that after a series of such operations we cannot return to the original set of points.
Prove that for all positive numbers $x$, $y$ and $z$ the inequality $$\sqrt[2]{x+\sqrt[3]{y+\sqrt[4]{z}}}\geqslant\sqrt[32]{xyz}$$ holds.

Two regular $10$-gons are given, and at each vertex of each of them some natural number is written. It is known that the sum of the numbers on each $10$-gon equals $99$. Prove that on both polygons one can mark several consecutive vertices (but not all) so that the sums of the marked numbers are equal.
A sequence $(a_k)$ consists of positive numbers and is such that $(a_{k+1}+k)a_k=1$ for every $k$. Prove that all its terms are irrational.

Points $D$, $E$ and $F$ are chosen on the sides $AC$, $AB$ and $BC$ of an isosceles triangle $ABC$ $(AB=BC)$ so that $DE=DF$ and moreover $AE+FC=AC$. Prove that the angles $\angle BAC$ and $\angle FDE$ are equal.

The digits $1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 7$ are written in the cells of the fourth column of a $6\times 7$ rectangular table. Can the other cells be filled with digits so that the seven-digit numbers formed in the rows form an arithmetic progression, and the six-digit numbers formed in the columns also form an arithmetic progression?
Prove that a square cannot be cut into isosceles triangles with vertex angle equal to $10^\circ$.

On the square $h8$ of a chessboard there is a stack of $n$ distinct checkers. Checkers may be taken off the stack and moved along the board one square down or to the left. It is forbidden to put one checker on another on any square except the square $a1$. For what largest $n$ can any stack on the square $a1$ (meaning the order of the checkers in the stack) be obtained from the original stack on the square $h8$?

$93$ teams took part in a round-robin volleyball tournament. It is known that whichever $19$ of them we take, among them there is a team that beat all the other $18$, and also a team that lost to all the other $18$. Prove that all teams scored different numbers of points.

A natural number is written on the board. Every second the sum of its digits standing in the even places of its decimal representation (the tens digit, the thousands digit, etc.) is added to it. Prove that sooner or later the number on the board stops changing.

Four points are marked inside a convex quadrilateral. Prove that on the perimeter of the quadrilateral there is a point the sum of whose distances to the vertices is greater than the sum of its distances to the marked points.

On an island whose population consists only of knights, who always tell the truth, and liars, who always lie, there is a research institute. Each of its employees once made two statements: a) In the institute there are not even ten people who work more than I do; b) At least a hundred people in the institute receive a higher salary than mine. It is known that the workloads of all the employees are different, and so are their salaries. How many people work at the institute?
Natural numbers $p$ and $q$ are such that $p\geqslant q$. The donkey Eeyore has $pq$ sticks from which he can form $p$ $q$-gons. Prove that from the same sticks Eeyore can form $q$ $p$-gons.
$AL$ is a bisector of a triangle $ABC$, and $K$ is a point on the side $AC$ such that $CK=CL$. The line $LK$ and the bisector of the angle $B$ meet at a point $P$. Prove that $AP=PL$.
It is known about natural numbers $a$, $b$, $c$ and $d$ that $$\frac{a^2+b}{a+c}=d.$$ Prove that $d\leqslant b+(c-1)^2$.

Two players play a game. The first player has thought of a number, and the second player in a move may name any $k$ distinct natural numbers not greater than $100$, after which the first player reports the sum of the thought number and one of the named numbers. For what largest $k$ can the second player sooner or later guess the thought number?

A square is divided into several rectangles so that every horizontal line meets exactly $n$ rectangles, and every vertical line exactly $m$ rectangles (only lines not containing sides of rectangles are considered). What is the smallest possible number of rectangles in the division?

Points $K$, $L$, $M$ and $N$ are taken on the sides $AB$, $BC$, $CD$ and $DA$ of an arbitrary quadrilateral $ABCD$ respectively. Denote by $S_1$, $S_2$, $S_3$ and $S_4$ the areas of the triangles $AKN$, $BKL$, $CLM$ and $DMN$ respectively. Prove that $$\sqrt[3]{S_1}+\sqrt[3]{S_2}+\sqrt[3]{S_3}+\sqrt[3]{S_4}\leqslant 2\sqrt[3]{S_{ABCD}}.$$

At points $A$ and $B$ lying on different sides of an angle, perpendiculars to the sides are erected; they meet the bisector of the angle at points $C$ and $D$. Prove that the midpoint of the segment $CD$ is equidistant from the points $A$ and $B$.
Natural numbers $a$, $b$ and $n>1$ are such that $(a+b)^n$ is divisible by $ab$. Prove that $a^{n-1}$ is divisible by $b$.

The segments joining a point $P$ lying inside a square $ABCD$ with the vertices divide the square into four triangles. Prove that the ratio of the areas of some two of them lies in the interval $[3/5;\ 5/3]$.
The number $1994$ is written on the board. Every second its largest prime divisor is added to the number on the board. Prove that at some moment this number will be divisible by $1995$.
In a non-isosceles acute-angled triangle $ABC$ a point $O$ is taken such that $\angle OBC=\angle OCB=20^\circ$. Moreover, $\angle BAO+\angle OCA=70^\circ$. Find the angle $A$.

Pluses and minuses are placed in the cells of a $1995\times 1995$ table. One may choose $1995$ cells no two of which lie in the same row or the same column, and change the signs in the chosen cells. Prove that by such operations one can achieve that at most $1994$ pluses remain in the table.

All sequences of natural numbers $(a_n)$ of length $1994$ with the following property are considered: $a_1=1$, $a_{n+1}\leqslant 1+a_n$. Prove that the number of such sequences with an even sum of terms equals the number of sequences with an odd sum of terms.

$200$ tennis players hold a tournament according to the Shvambranian system. This means that every day before the next games they line up in non-increasing order of the points scored by that moment, and then split into $100$ pairs of players standing next to each other. Prove that if the tournament lasts long enough, then on some day the results of some two players will differ by more than $50$ points. (There are no draws in tennis; a player gets $1$ point for a win and $0$ for a loss.)
Let $a, b>0$ and $a+b\leqslant 2$. Prove that $$\frac{a}{b+ab}+\frac{b}{a+ab}\geqslant 1.$$

A triangle $ABC$ and points $D$ and $E$ such that $\angle ADB=\angle BEC=90^\circ$ are given in the plane. Prove that the length of the segment $DE$ does not exceed the semiperimeter of the triangle $ABC$. (The figure shows only one of the possible positions of the points.)

Solve in natural numbers the equation $x^{(2^x)}=y^{(512^y)}$.
Prove that the number of ways to cut a rectangle into three-cell corners (L-shaped pieces: a $2\times 2$ square without one cell) is always even.

In a quadrilateral $ABCD$, points $R$ and $T$ are taken on the sides $BC$ and $AD$ respectively. $P$ is the intersection point of the segments $BT$ and $AR$; $S$ is the intersection point of the segments $CT$ and $DR$. It turned out that $PRST$ is a parallelogram. Prove that $AB\parallel CD$.
$a$, $b$, $c$ are natural numbers such that $a-b$ is a prime number and $3c^2=c(a+b)+ab$. Prove that $8c+1$ is a perfect square.

A state has $2000$ cities. Some pairs of cities are connected by roads so that one can drive from any city to any other. Prove that this state can be divided into several republics (possibly just one) so that in each republic one can drive from any city to any other city of this republic in a unique way without leaving it. (Each republic must contain at least two cities.)
$p$ and $q$ are prime numbers such that $p^2+1$ is divisible by $q$, and $q^2-1$ is divisible by $p$. Prove that $p+q+1$ is a composite number.
Let $a, b, c>0$. Prove the inequality $$\left(\frac{a+2b}{c}\right)^2+\left(\frac{b+2c}{a}\right)^2+\left(\frac{c+2a}{b}\right)^2\geqslant 27.$$

Two intersecting circles are given in the plane. The point $A$ is one of the two intersection points of these circles. In each circle a diameter is drawn parallel to the tangent at the point $A$ to the other circle, and these diameters do not intersect. Prove that the endpoints of these diameters lie on one circle.

$1995$ points are given in the plane, and some pairs of points are joined by segments. The points are initially coloured in two colours. Every minute (simultaneously) those points that are joined to an even number of points of the same colour change their colour. Prove that the original colouring cannot be obtained again after an odd number of minutes.
Let $M$ be the set of values of the polynomial $x^2+1$ at integer points. Prove that the set $M$ does not contain any infinite (non-constant) geometric progression.

A rectangle is divided into dominoes (that is, $1\times 2$ rectangles). Prove that its cells can be coloured in two colours so that every domino of the given division contains cells of different colours, but in every other division of this rectangle into dominoes there is a domino containing two cells of the same colour.

$H$ is the orthocentre of an acute-angled triangle $ABC$, and $D$ is the midpoint of the side $AC$. The line passing through $H$ perpendicular to the segment $DH$ meets the sides $AB$ and $BC$ at points $E$ and $F$. Prove that $HE=HF$.
Does there exist an increasing sequence of natural numbers $\{b_n\}_{n=1}^\infty$ such that for all natural $n$ the sum of the digits of the number $b_{n+1}^5$ equals the number $b_n^5$?

Several one-digit numbers are written on the board. One may compute the sum of all the numbers and write the last digit of the result on the board in place of one of the numbers. Prove that after several such operations the original set of numbers can be obtained again.
$50$ numbers are chosen among the natural numbers from $1$ to $99$. It is known that no two of them add up to $99$ or to $100$. Prove that the chosen numbers are all the numbers from $50$ to $99$.

$M$ is the intersection point of the diagonals of a trapezoid $ABCD$. A point $P$ is chosen on the base $BC$ such that $\angle APM=\angle DPM$. Prove that the distance from the point $C$ to the line $AP$ equals the distance from the point $B$ to the line $DP$.

In a group of several people, some people are acquainted with each other and some are not. Every evening one of them holds a dinner for all his acquaintances and introduces them to each other. After every person has held at least one dinner, it turned out that some two people are still not acquainted. Prove that they will not manage to get acquainted at the next dinner either.

$M$ is the intersection point of the diagonals of a cyclic quadrilateral, $N$ is the intersection point of its midlines, and $O$ is the centre of the circumscribed circle. Prove that $OM\geqslant ON$ (a midline is the segment joining the midpoints of opposite sides).

Prove that for every polynomial $p(x)$ of degree ten with integer coefficients there is a non-constant integer arithmetic progression, infinite in both directions, that contains no term of the form $p(k)$, where $k$ is an integer.

There are $n$ parking places along a one-way street. $n$ cars enter the street one after another (numbered from $1$ to $n$ in increasing order). Each driver drives to his favourite parking place and parks there if it is not occupied; otherwise he drives on to the first free place and parks there, and if all places further on are occupied, he leaves (for good). Call the list $a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n$ of the favourite parking places of the first, second, $\ldots$, $n$-th driver a preference sequence. How many preference sequences are there for which all drivers manage to park?

$BD$ is the bisector of the angle $B$ of a triangle $ABC$. The circumscribed circle of the triangle $BDC$ meets the segment $AB$ at a point $E$, and the circumscribed circle of the triangle $ABD$ meets the segment $BC$ at a point $F$. Prove that $AE=CF$.

Natural numbers are placed in a $10\times 10$ table. It is known that for any five rows and any five columns the sum of the $25$ numbers standing at their intersections is even. Prove that all numbers in the table are even.
Prove that there do not exist natural numbers $a$ and $b$ such that for any distinct prime numbers $p$ and $q$ greater than $1000$ the number $ap+bq$ is also prime.

In a triangle $ABC$ the angle $A$ equals $60^\circ$. A point $O$ is taken inside the triangle such that $\angle AOB=\angle AOC=120^\circ$. The points $D$ and $E$ are the midpoints of the sides $AB$ and $AC$. Prove that the quadrilateral $ADOE$ is cyclic.

A country has $2000$ cities, every two of which are connected by a road. Construction organizations submitted all possible projects of introducing one-way traffic on all roads. The Ministry of Transport rejected all projects that did not make it possible to get from any city to any other. Prove that nevertheless more than half of the projects remained.

Four natural numbers $m$, $n$, $m$, $n$ are written on the board. The generalized Euclidean algorithm is applied to this ordered quadruple: if the numbers $(x,y,u,v)$ are written on the board and $x>y$, they are replaced by $(x-y,y,u+v,v)$, and if $x<y$, by $(x,y-x,u,v+u)$. The algorithm stops when the numbers of the first pair become equal (at that moment they are equal to the greatest common divisor of $m$ and $n$). Prove that the arithmetic mean of the numbers of the second pair at that moment equals the least common multiple of $m$ and $n$.

A set of geometric figures consists of red equilateral triangles and blue quadrilaterals all of whose angles are greater than $80^\circ$ but less than $100^\circ$. A convex polygon all of whose angles are greater than $60^\circ$ was assembled from figures of this set. Prove that the number of (entirely) red sides of this polygon is divisible by $3$.

The natural numbers from $1$ to $n^2$ are placed in the cells of an $n\times n$ table. After placing the next number in a free cell, the sum of the numbers already placed in the row and the column containing this cell is written on the board. When the whole table is filled, the sum of the numbers written on the board is computed. Give an example of a way of placing the numbers for which this sum takes the smallest possible value.

Trees of equal height grow along the sixtieth parallel. If they all fall to the west, the total length of the parts of the sixtieth parallel covered by more than five trees will be $100$ km. Prove that if all the trees fall to the east, the total length of the parts of the sixtieth parallel covered more than five times will also be $100$ km.

The points $K$ and $N$ are the midpoints of the sides $AB$ and $CD$ of a quadrilateral $ABCD$. The segments $BN$ and $KC$ meet at a point $O$. The intersection points of the lines $AO$ and $DO$ with the side $BC$ divide the segment $BC$ into three equal parts. Prove that $ABCD$ is a parallelogram.
A root of the trinomial $ax^2+bx+b$ was multiplied by a root of the trinomial $ax^2+ax+b$, and the product $1$ was obtained. Find these roots.

The cells of a $100\times 100$ square are coloured black and white so that every $1\times 2$ rectangle contains at least one black cell, and every $1\times 6$ rectangle contains two black cells standing next to each other. What is the smallest possible number of black cells in this square?
A sequence of natural numbers $\{x_n\}$ is defined by the relations $$x_1=2,\qquad x_{n+1}=2x_n^2-1.$$ Prove that for all $n$ the numbers $x_n$ and $n$ are coprime.

In a trapezoid $ABCD$ the diagonal $AC$ equals the sum of the bases $AB$ and $CD$. The point $M$ is the midpoint of the side $BC$. The point $B'$ is symmetric to the point $B$ with respect to the line $AM$. Prove that $\angle ABD=\angle CB'D$.

$3n$ people live in the town of Neznakomsk, and any two inhabitants have a common acquaintance. Prove that one can point out $n$ people such that each of the others is acquainted with at least one of these $n$ people.
The inscribed circle was projected onto the sides of a triangle. Prove that the six endpoints of the projections lie on one circle.
$a$ and $b$ are integers. Prove that $$\left|\frac{a+b}{a-b}\right|^{ab}\geqslant 1.$$
Prove that every natural number has at least as many divisors whose decimal representation ends in $1$ or $9$ as divisors whose decimal representation ends in $3$ or $7$.
Prove that the opposite corners of a $142\times 857$ grid rectangle cannot be joined by a five-link broken line with vertices at grid nodes whose link lengths are in the ratio $2:3:4:5:6$.
Do there exist $100$ natural numbers such that the sum of the fourth powers of any four of them is divisible by the product of these four?

$B'$ is the point of the circumscribed circle of an acute-angled triangle $ABC$ diametrically opposite to the vertex $B$. $I$ is the centre of the inscribed circle of the triangle $ABC$, and $M$ is the point of tangency of the inscribed circle with the side $AC$. Points $K$ and $L$ are chosen on the sides $AB$ and $BC$ respectively such that $KB=MC$, $LB=AM$. Prove that the lines $B'I$ and $KL$ are perpendicular.
Can a $1997\times 1997$ grid square be cut (along the cells) into squares with sides greater than $30$ cells?

Natural numbers are placed at the vertices of a regular $1997$-gon. One may add $2$ to any of the numbers and simultaneously subtract one from each of the two numbers at distance exactly $k$ $(1\leqslant k\leqslant 998)$ from it clockwise and counterclockwise; the number $k$ is then written on the board. After several operations all vertices again carry the original numbers. Prove that by this time the sum of the squares of the numbers written on the board is divisible by $1997$.
The numbers $x$, $y$, $z$, $t$ satisfy the inequality $$(x+y+z+t)^2\geqslant 4(x^2+y^2+z^2+t^2).$$ Prove that there exists a real number $a$ such that $$(x-a)(y-a)+(z-a)(t-a)=0.$$

The numbers from $1$ to $100$ are placed around a circle (in arbitrary order). For every three consecutive numbers their sum was computed. Prove that some two of the computed sums differ by at least $3$.

In a triangle $ABC$, the point $M$ is the midpoint of the side $BC$, and $AA_1$, $BB_1$, $CC_1$ are the altitudes. The lines $AB$ and $A_1B_1$ meet at a point $X$, and the lines $MC_1$ and $AC$ meet at a point $Y$. Prove that $XY\parallel BC$.
Find all integer solutions of the equation $$p^2+q^2+pq=15r^2.$$

In the decimal expansion of an irreducible fraction $m/n$, every digit after the decimal point except the first is less than the sum of its two neighbouring digits by one and the same natural number $k$. Prove that $n\leqslant 819$.

The point $M$ is the midpoint of the side $AC$ of a triangle $ABC$. A point $K$ is chosen on the segment $AM$, a point $L$ on the segment $BM$, and a point $N$ on the segment $BK$. It turned out that $KL\parallel AB$, $MN\parallel BC$ and $CL=2KM$. Prove that $CN$ is the bisector of the angle $ACL$.
A country has $2n$ cities and several airlines. Any four cities are connected with each other by at most four airlines. What is the largest possible number of airlines in this country?
With how many zeros can the number $1^n+2^n+3^n+4^n$ $(n\in\mathbb{N})$ end?

The diagonals of a parallelogram $ABCD$ meet at a point $O$. The circle circumscribed about the triangle $ABO$ meets the side $AD$ at a point $E$. The circle circumscribed about the triangle $DOE$ meets the segment $BE$ at a point $F$. Prove that $\angle BCA=\angle FCD$.

A non-self-intersecting closed broken line not passing through the nodes of the grid is drawn on a sheet of squared paper. At least $91$ nodes lie in the region bounded by the broken line. Prove that the broken line meets the grid lines in at least $40$ points.

Prove that the number of natural numbers $\overline{a_ma_{m-1}\ldots a_1}$ $(m>1998)$ such that $$\overline{a_ma_{m-1}\ldots a_1}=\overline{a_ma_{m-1}\ldots a_{1999}}^{\,2}+\overline{a_{1998}a_{1997}\ldots a_1}^{\,2}$$ is even.

All natural numbers from $1$ to $100$ are placed in a $10\times 10$ square. In each row the third largest number (counting from the largest) was marked. Prove that the sum of all marked numbers is not less than the sum of the numbers in some row.

Prove that the projections of the intersection point of the diagonals of a cyclic quadrilateral onto two of its opposite sides are symmetric with respect to the line joining the midpoints of the other two opposite sides of this quadrilateral.

A set $M$ consists of $n$ points of the plane, no three of which lie on one line. For every triangle with vertices in $M$ the number of points of $M$ inside it was counted. Prove that the arithmetic mean of all the numbers found does not exceed $n/4$.

Two piles of matches lie on a very large table. The first pile has $2^{100}$ matches, the second $3^{100}$. Two players alternately take matches from the piles. In one move a player may take $k$ matches from one pile and $m$ from the other so that $|k^2-m^2|\leqslant 1000$. The player who takes the last match wins. Who wins with correct play?
Prove that there are no natural numbers $x$ and $y$ and prime number $p$ such that $\sqrt[3]{x}+\sqrt[3]{y}=\sqrt[3]{p}$.

$45$ languages are used on the island of New Babylonia, and every inhabitant knows at least five of them. It is known that any two inhabitants can talk to each other, possibly through several interpreters. Prove that then any two islanders can talk to each other using the services of at most $15$ interpreters.

In a non-isosceles triangle $ABC$ the bisectors $AA_1$ and $CC_1$ are drawn, and the midpoints $K$ and $L$ of the sides $AB$ and $BC$ respectively are marked. The point $P$ is the foot of the perpendicular dropped from the vertex $A$ to the line $CC_1$, and the point $Q$ is the foot of the perpendicular dropped from the vertex $C$ to the line $AA_1$. Prove that the lines $KP$ and $LQ$ meet on the side $AC$.

A pile of $123456789$ grains of sand lies in a sandbox. Dima and Katya play the following game. In one move one may take from any pile any number of grains greater than $1$ that is a divisor of the number of grains in this pile, and form a separate pile of them. Katya moves first. The player who cannot move loses. Who wins with correct play?

A point $K$ is taken on the side $BC$ of an acute-angled triangle $ABC$. The bisector of the angle $CAK$ meets the circle circumscribed about the triangle $ABC$ a second time at a point $L$. Prove that if the line $LK$ is perpendicular to the segment $AB$, then either $AK=KB$ or $AK=AC$.
Natural numbers $a$, $b$, $c$ and $d$ are such that $$a^2+b^2+ab=c^2+d^2+cd.$$ Prove that the number $a+b+c+d$ is composite.

In Müller's office there is a safe whose cells are arranged as a $100\times 100$ square. Important secret materials are kept in $25$ of the cells. Stirlitz managed to find out in which ones and to send the Centre a coded message in the form of a sequence of $25$ numbers from $1$ to $100$. Prove that Stirlitz and the Centre could have agreed on a coding method in advance so that the Centre's staff, having studied the message, could choose $400$ cells among which the $25$ required ones are certainly contained.

The real numbers $x_0$, $x_1$, $\ldots$, $x_n$ are known to satisfy $x_0>x_1>\ldots>x_n$. Prove the inequality $$x_0+\frac{1}{x_0-x_1}+\frac{1}{x_1-x_2}+\ldots+\frac{1}{x_{n-1}-x_n}\geqslant x_n+2n.$$

The quadratic trinomial $f(x)=x^2+ax+b$ with integer coefficients has value at $0$ of absolute value at most $800$. It is also known that $f(120)$ is a prime number. Prove that it has no integer roots.

For which $n\geqslant 3$ can the numbers from $1$ to $n$ be placed at the vertices of a regular $n$-gon so that the following property holds: for any three vertices $A$, $B$ and $C$ such that $AB=AC$, the number at the vertex $A$ is either greater than both numbers at the vertices $B$ and $C$ or less than both of them?

Points $A_1$, $B_1$ and $C_1$ are chosen on the sides $BC$, $AC$ and $AB$ of an isosceles triangle $ABC$ $(AB=BC)$. It is known that $\angle BC_1A_1=\angle CA_1B_1=\angle A$. $P$ is the intersection point of the segments $BB_1$ and $CC_1$. Prove that the quadrilateral $AB_1PC_1$ is cyclic.
Find the set of values of the expression $$f(x,y,z)=\left\{\frac{xyz}{xy+yz+zx}\right\}$$ for natural $x$, $y$ and $z$. (Here $\{s\}$ denotes the fractional part of $s$.)

$AL$ is a bisector of a triangle $ABC$. Parallel lines $b$ and $c$, equidistant from the vertex $A$, are drawn through the vertices $B$ and $C$. Points $M$ and $N$ are chosen on the lines $b$ and $c$ such that the segments $LM$ and $LN$ meet the sides $AB$ and $AC$ respectively and are bisected by them. Prove that $LM=LN$.

Prove that the number of ways to cut a $998\times 999$ rectangle into corners (L-shaped pieces of three unit squares, i.e. a $2\times 2$ square without one cell) does not exceed the number of ways to cut a $1998\times 2000$ rectangle into corners so that no two corners form a $2\times 3$ rectangle.

A convex $n$-gon $(n>3)$ is divided into triangles by non-intersecting diagonals. Prove that one can mark $n-1$ segments among the drawn diagonals and the sides of the polygon so that no set of marked segments forms a closed broken line and no vertex is the endpoint of exactly two marked segments.

Two rows of $1000$ trees each were planted on the two sides of a road. A plate was nailed to each tree stating how many oaks there are among this tree and its left and right neighbours (for the end trees, among the tree itself and its only neighbour). It turned out that the two sequences of numbers on the plates coincide. Prove that in both rows the oaks grow in the same places.

In an acute-angled triangle $ABC$ the altitudes $AA_1$ and $CC_1$ are drawn. A point $D$ is chosen on the altitude $AA_1$ such that $A_1D=C_1D$. The point $E$ is the midpoint of the side $AC$. Prove that the points $A$, $C_1$, $D$ and $E$ lie on one circle.
Let $F(x)=x^{2000}-x^{1000}+1$. Do there exist distinct natural numbers $a_1$, $a_2$, $\ldots$, $a_{2001}$ such that $F(a_i)F(a_j)$ is divisible by $a_ia_j$ for all $i\neq j$?

$101$ lines are drawn in the coordinate plane, and all their points of intersection with each other are marked. Can it happen that on each of the drawn lines there lie $50$ marked points with positive first coordinates and $50$ with negative ones?

The natural numbers $1, 2, \ldots, 2000$ are written on the board. Two players move alternately according to the following rules: one may erase any two numbers $a$ and $b$ and write $a^b$ instead of them. After some time one number remains on the board. The first player wins if it ends in $2$, $7$ or $8$, and the second player otherwise. Who wins with correct play?

An excircle of a triangle $ABC$ touches its side $BC$ at a point $K$ and the extension of the side $AB$ at a point $L$. Another excircle touches the extensions of the sides $AB$ and $BC$ at points $M$ and $N$ respectively. The lines $KL$ and $MN$ meet at a point $X$. Prove that $CX$ is the bisector of the angle $ACN$.

The complexity of a sequence $a_1$, $a_2$, $\ldots$ consisting of zeros and ones is the smallest natural number $k$ such that for some natural numbers $\varepsilon_1$, $\varepsilon_2$, $\ldots$, $\varepsilon_k$ every term $a_n$ of the sequence with $n>k$ has the same parity as $\varepsilon_1a_{n-1}+\varepsilon_2a_{n-2}+\ldots+\varepsilon_ka_{n-k}$. The sequence $a_1$, $a_2$, $\ldots$ has complexity $1000$. What can the complexity of the sequence $1-a_1$, $1-a_2$, $\ldots$ be? (Give all possible values and prove that there are no others.)

Do there exist four quadratic trinomials such that, whatever order they are written in, one can find a number whose substitution into these trinomials gives values written in strictly increasing order?

$S_1$ and $S_2$ are two circles having no common points. A common (external) tangent touches them at points $A$ and $B$. A circle $S_3$ passes through $A$ and $B$ and meets $S_1$ and $S_2$ a second time at points $C$ and $D$ respectively. $K$ is the intersection point of the lines tangent to $S_1$ and $S_2$ at the points $C$ and $D$. Prove that $KC=KD$.

Several cells of a $1001\times 1001$ board are marked so that no two adjacent cells are marked, but the number of cells sharing a side with marked cells is less than the number of marked cells. How many cells are marked?
Do there exist $1000$ natural numbers such that the greatest common divisors of all possible sets of these numbers (of two, of three, $\ldots$, of a thousand) are pairwise distinct?

In an acute-angled triangle $ABC$ the altitudes $AA_1$, $BB_1$ and $CC_1$ are drawn. Points $A_2$ and $C_2$ were chosen on the segment $A_1C_1$ such that the segment $B_1A_2$ is bisected by the altitude $CC_1$ and meets the altitude $AA_1$ at a point $K$, and the segment $B_1C_2$ is bisected by the altitude $AA_1$ and meets the altitude $CC_1$ at a point $L$. Prove that $KL\parallel AC$.
$100$ points are placed in the coordinate plane. Prove that there are at most $2025=45^2$ rectangles with vertices at these points and sides parallel to the axes.
$a$ and $b$ are distinct natural numbers such that $a^2+b$ is divisible by $b^2+a$ and $b^2+a$ is a power of a prime number. Find these numbers.

A network of airlines is called reliable if, after the closure of any airport, one can fly from any open airport to any other (possibly with changes). A country has $2000$ airports and initially no airlines. Two airline companies alternately introduce new non-stop airlines. The company after whose move the network of airlines becomes reliable loses. Which of the companies wins with correct play?

All cells of a $10\times 10$ board are painted white. Fedya and Yura alternately (Fedya begins) repaint one white cell black. The player after whose move there are no two white cells sharing a side left on the board loses. Who wins with correct play?

Call a quadratic trinomial good if it has two distinct real roots and its coefficients are pairwise distinct numbers. Do there exist $10$ positive numbers such that one can find $500$ good quadratic trinomials all of whose coefficients are among these numbers?
In a convex pentagon $ABCDE$, $AB=BC$, $CD=DE$ and $\angle A=\angle C=\angle E<90^\circ$. Prove that this pentagon is circumscribed (has an inscribed circle).

$a$, $b$ and $c$ are natural numbers for which $$(a^2-1,\ b^2-1,\ c^2-1)=1.$$ Prove that $$(ab+c,\ bc+a,\ ca+b)=(a,b,c).$$ (As usual, $(x,y,z)$ denotes the greatest common divisor of the numbers $x$, $y$ and $z$.)

The points $A_1$, $B_1$ and $C_1$ are the midpoints of the sides $BC$, $CA$ and $AB$ of a triangle $ABC$. Points $E$ and $F$ are marked on the midlines $C_1B_1$ and $A_1B_1$ respectively so that the line $BE$ contains the bisector of the angle $AEB_1$, and the line $BF$ contains the bisector of the angle $CFB_1$. Prove that the bisectors of the angles $ABC$ and $FBE$ coincide.
Solve in natural numbers the equation $k^m+m^n=k^n+1$.

$300$ students take part in an international olympiad. Each student speaks exactly two of the six official languages of the olympiad, and each language is spoken by exactly one hundred students (it is known that the students speak only the official languages). Prove that the organizers can seat the participants at a round table so that no two neighbours speak a common language.

Natural numbers not exceeding $10$ are written in a $10\times 10$ table. The numbers in any two cells adjacent by a side or a corner are coprime. Prove that some number occurs in the table at least $17$ times.

The bisectors of the angles $A$ and $B$ of a convex quadrilateral $ABCD$ meet at a point $P$, and the bisectors of the angles $C$ and $D$ at a point $Q$ different from $P$. The line $PQ$ passes through the midpoint of the side $AB$. Prove that $\angle ABC=\angle BAD$ or $\angle ABC+\angle BAD=180^\circ$.

Do there exist quadratic trinomials $f$ and $g$ with leading coefficients equal to one such that for every integer $n$ the number $f(n)g(n)$ is an integer, while the numbers $f(n)$, $g(n)$ and $f(n)+g(n)$ are not integers?

$10$ points numbered from $1$ to $10$ are marked in the plane. One may choose any rectangular coordinate system and write the numbers of the points in a row in increasing order of their first coordinates (provided that all first coordinates are distinct). What is the largest number of permutations of the numbers from $1$ to $10$ that can be obtained in this way from one set of points in the plane?

A natural number is written on the board. Two players move alternately, and each in his move replaces the number $n$ written on the board by the number $n-1$ or $\left[\frac{n+1}{2}\right]$ (square brackets denote the integer part). The player who first writes the number $1$ on the board wins. Who wins with correct play, the first player or his partner, if at the start of the game the number on the board is $1\,000\,000$?

The altitudes of an acute-angled triangle $ABC$ meet at a point $H$. A point $K$ is such that the circumscribed circles of the triangles $BHK$ and $CHK$ are tangent to the line $BC$. The point $D$ is the foot of the altitude dropped from the vertex $B$ to the side $AC$. Prove that the point $A$ is equidistant from the lines $KB$ and $KD$.
Let $n$, $m$ and $k$ be natural numbers with $n>1$. Prove that $(\sigma(n))^k\neq n^m$, where $\sigma(n)$ is the sum of all natural divisors of the number $n$.

In a chess club visitors can play chess with each other or with a computer. Yesterday there were $n$ people in the club, each of them played at most $n$ games, and any two who did not play each other played at most $n$ games in total. Prove that at most $\frac{n(n+1)}{2}$ games were played in all.

A natural number is called symmetric if it does not change when its decimal representation is reversed (for example, $2002$ is a symmetric number). Prove that if $a$ and $3a$ are symmetric numbers, then $2a$ is also a symmetric number.

Every employee of the company "Kaka-Kola" who has an even number of acquaintances among the employees sent each of them a letter, and each of the other employees of the company sent a letter to everybody he does not know. Teddy received $99$ letters. Prove that he will receive at least one more letter.

On the extension of each side $A_kA_{k+1}$ of a regular polygon $A_1A_2\ldots A_n$ beyond the point $A_{k+1}$, a point $B_{k+1}$ is marked. It turned out that the perimeters of all the triangles $A_kB_kB_{k+1}$ are equal. Prove that the triangles themselves are also equal (congruent).

Harry has one mouse and very, very many frogs. Harry can turn frogs into mice or vice versa according to the following rule: if the numbers of mice and frogs are not equal, then the number of those animals of which there were fewer than half is doubled. After Harry managed to perform this operation $17$ times in a row, for the first time there were twice as many mice as frogs. How many animals did Harry have?

Kostya laid out from sticks of integer lengths a $10\times 10$ square (together with its boundary) divided into $1\times 1$ cells. The sticks do not intersect at interior points. What is the smallest number of sticks of unit length that could have been used?

$a$, $b$, $c$ are positive numbers. Fedya found the sum of the positive roots of the equations $$x^2=ax+b,\quad x^2=bx+c\quad\text{and}\quad x^2=cx+a,$$ and Yura found the sum of the positive roots of the equations $$x^2=ax+a,\quad x^2=bx+b\quad\text{and}\quad x^2=cx+c.$$ These sums turned out to be different. Which of the boys has the greater sum?

A point $K$ is marked on the side $AC$ of a triangle $ABC$ such that $AK=2KC$ and $\angle ABK=2\angle KBC$. $F$ is the midpoint of the side $AC$, and $L$ is the projection of $A$ onto $BK$. Prove that the lines $FL$ and $BC$ are perpendicular.
The number $\overline{a0a0\ldots a0b0c0c0\ldots c0c}$ (the digits $a$ and $c$ are written $1001$ times each) is divisible by $37$. Prove that $b=a+c$.
In a trapezoid $ABCD$ the length of the lateral side $AB$ equals the sum of the lengths of the bases $AD$ and $BC$. Prove that the bisectors of the angles $A$ and $B$ meet on the side $CD$.
Can the sum of the pairwise distances between the vertices of a tree with $25$ vertices be equal to $1225$?

The numbers from $5$ to $10$ are written on the board. Once a minute Kostya erases the $3$ or $4$ smallest numbers and appends the $7$ or $8$ numbers following the largest one. Prove that the sum of the numbers on the board will never be a power of three.
For what largest $\alpha$ can any real numbers $$0=a_1\leqslant a_2\leqslant\ldots\leqslant a_{11}=1$$ be divided into two groups whose arithmetic means differ by at least $\alpha$?
problems.proposer: M. A. Lifshits, Yu. Lifshits, F. Petrov

problems.problem: Let $O$ be the centre of the circumscribed circle of an acute-angled non-isosceles triangle $ABC$, let the point $C_1$ be symmetric to $C$ with respect to $O$, let $D$ be the midpoint of the side $AB$, and let $K$ be the centre of the circumscribed circle of the triangle $ODC_1$. Prove that the point $O$ bisects the segment of the line $OK$ lying inside the angle $ACB$.

Can the numbers from $1$ to $1717$ be placed in a $17\times 101$ rectangle so that in every figure of the shape consisting of two cells side by side and two more cells side by side in the row below, shifted one cell to the right (a "skew" four-cell piece of a $2\times 3$ rectangle: upper row cells 1–2, lower row cells 2–3), lying entirely in the rectangle, the sum of the numbers is divisible by $17$ or by $101$?

A polygon $F$, no three of whose vertices lie on one line, can be divided into triangles by non-intersecting diagonals in two ways. Prove that some four vertices of $F$ form a convex quadrilateral lying entirely in $F$.
Prove that for every positive number $x$ the inequality $2x^9+9x^8\leqslant 9x^{10}+2$ holds.

Prove that there exists a set of $100$ pairwise distinct natural numbers such that for every division of the numbers of this set into two non-empty groups, the sum of the numbers in one of the groups is divisible by the sum of the numbers in the other group.

A convex hexagon $ABCDEF$ is given in which $\angle CAB=\angle FBA$, $\angle ECD=\angle BDC$, $\angle AEF=\angle DFE$, $\angle EAC=\angle FBD$, $\angle ACE=\angle BDF$, $\angle CEA=\angle DFB$. Prove that the hexagon formed by the intersection of the segments $AC$, $BD$, $CE$, $DF$, $EA$ and $FB$ is circumscribed (has an inscribed circle).

There are $30$ piles of matches on a table: with $100, 101, 102, \ldots, 129$ matches. Dima and Sasha play the following game: a move consists of either taking one match from any pile or merging into one pile two non-empty piles whose numbers of matches have the same parity. The player who cannot move loses. Who wins with correct play if Dima begins?

$BM$ is a median of an acute-angled triangle $ABC$. The tangent at the point $A$ to the circle circumscribed about the triangle $ABM$ and the tangent at the point $C$ to the circle circumscribed about the triangle $BCM$ meet at a point $D$. Prove that the point $K$ symmetric to the point $D$ with respect to the line $AC$ lies on the line $BM$.

Dima and Sasha place the numbers from $1$ to $64$ on a chessboard in all possible ways. For each arrangement Dima computes the product of the numbers in every row and then adds up the $8$ products obtained. Sasha computes the product of the numbers in each of the $15$ diagonals parallel to the diagonal $h1$–$a8$ (in particular, the first and the fifteenth diagonals consist of only one number) and then adds up his $15$ products. Prove that for at least half of all possible arrangements Dima's sum is greater than Sasha's.

Find all quadratic trinomials $f(x)=x^2+px+q$ with non-negative integer coefficients such that whenever for some natural numbers $a$ and $b$ the numbers $f(a)$ and $f(b)$ are coprime, the numbers $a$ and $b$ are also coprime.

Ten students stand in a row. Every minute some two neighbouring students swap places. After some time it turned out that each of the students had been both in the first and in the last place. Prove that at least $65$ minutes have passed.

A quadrilateral $ABCD$ is given whose diagonals meet at a point $L$. On the side $AD$ there is a point $F$ such that $\angle FBC=2\angle FAC$, $\angle FCB=2\angle FDB$ and $\angle AFB=\angle DFC$. Prove that the lines $AB$, $CD$ and $FL$ meet at one point.

Two mad geometers alternately mark points in the plane, and after each move any three marked points must form a triangle of area at least $1$ and at most $1000$. The player who cannot move loses. Which of the geometers has a winning strategy?
Prove that for every natural $n$ the number $n!$ has the following property: to any of its divisors other than $n!$ itself one can add a divisor of $n!$ so that the sum is again a divisor of $n!$.
problems.proposer: A. Golovanov, A. Khrabrov, D. Rostovsky, S. Ivanov

problems.problem: The edges of a graph are coloured in four colours so that in every path of three edges the first and the third edges have different colours (the beginning and the end of the path may coincide). Prove that the vertices of this graph can be coloured in five colours so that any two vertices joined by an edge have different colours.
problems.proposer: S. Berlov, D. Karpov, A. Pastor

problems.problem: The point $K$ is the midpoint of the cevian $AD$ of a triangle $ABC$. A point $X$ on the segment $KC$ is such that $\angle ABK=\angle XBC$. It turned out that $KX\cdot BD=CX\cdot CD$. Prove that $\angle BAX=\angle BCX$.

Father Frost has $n$ distinct presents and several identical sacks. Each sack contains exactly two objects (two sacks, two presents, or a sack and a present). In particular, the single sack that Father Frost carries on his shoulder also contains two objects. In how many ways can the presents be distributed among the sacks?

A teacher wrote $4$ distinct natural numbers on the board and asked the children to multiply the first two and the last two. But the girl Masha mixed everything up and added the first two and also the last two. Nevertheless she obtained the same answers as the excellent pupil Katya. Which numbers did the teacher write on the board?

An acute-angled triangle $ABC$ is given. $B_1$, $C_1$ are the feet of the altitudes from the vertices $B$, $C$ respectively. The point $D$ is the foot of the perpendicular from $B_1$ to $AB$, and $E$ is the intersection point of the perpendicular dropped from the point $D$ to the side $BC$ with the segment $BB_1$. Prove that the line $EC_1$ is parallel to $AC$.
A $25$-digit number without nines in its decimal representation is given. Prove that one can increase two of its equal digits by $1$ so that the resulting number is not divisible by $7$.

$k$ cells are marked in a $100\times 100$ square so that for every cutting of the square along grid lines into two rectangles, one of the rectangles contains at least $100$ marked cells. For what smallest value of $k$ is this possible?
Three prime numbers are such that the product of any two of them is a perfect square increased by $6$. Prove that the sum of these prime numbers is a square increased by $9$.

In a convex quadrilateral $ABCD$ there are points $K$ and $L$ on the sides $AB$ and $BC$ respectively such that $\angle ADK=\angle CDL$. The segments $AL$ and $CK$ meet at a point $P$. Prove that $\angle ADP=\angle BDC$.

The club "National Wealth" has $15$ oligarchs, some of whom are business partners of each other. Analysing the financial results of $2003$, the Audit Chamber noted that at the beginning of the year the fortune of each member of the club was at least a quarter of the total fortune of all his partners, while already in December the fortune of each member of the club had become less than a quarter of the total fortune of all his partners. Prove that some oligarch established new business contacts in $2003$.
Prove that $\overline{xy}\cdot\overline{yz}\cdot\overline{zx}\neq\overline{yx}\cdot\overline{zy}\cdot\overline{xz}$ if the digits $x$, $y$, $z$, $0$ are pairwise distinct.
Some $n$ cells of an $n\times n$ square are painted. For what largest $k$ is there certainly a grid rectangle of perimeter $k$ containing no painted cells?

Isosceles triangles $AFB$ and $BLC$ are constructed on the sides $AB$ and $BC$ of an acute-angled triangle $ABC$ as bases, one of them lying inside the triangle $ABC$ and the other constructed outwards. Moreover, $\angle AFB=\angle BLC$ and $\angle CAF=\angle ACL$. Prove that the line $FL$ cuts off an isosceles triangle from the angle $ABC$.

$120$ numbers are written in a row. Seryozha may erase several numbers standing consecutively (but not all of them) and write in place of each of them the arithmetic mean of the erased numbers. Can he always achieve that all the numbers become equal?
Natural numbers $n$, $m$, $k$ are such that the numbers $5^n-2$ and $2^k-5$ are divisible by $5^m-2^m$. Prove that $n$ and $m$ are coprime.

A point $D$ is chosen on the minor arc $AC$ of the circumscribed circle of an acute-angled triangle $ABC$. On the side $AC$ there is a point $E$ such that $DE=AE$. On the line through $E$ parallel to $AB$, a point $F$ is marked such that $CF=BF$. Prove that $D$, $E$, $C$, $F$ lie on one circle.
Prove the inequality $$\frac{ab}{3a+b}+\frac{bc}{b+2c}+\frac{ac}{c+2a}\leqslant\frac{2a+20b+27c}{49}$$ for positive $a$, $b$, $c$.

A positive number not exceeding $1$ is written at every point of the plane. It is known that for every square with side $1$ the sums of the numbers at its opposite vertices are equal. Prove that all the numbers written in the plane are equal.
Natural numbers $a$, $b$ and $c$ are given. Prove the inequality $$\gcd(a,b)+\gcd(a,b+c)\leqslant a+c.$$
Prove that there do not exist four pairwise distinct quadratic trinomials with leading coefficients equal to $1$ such that the sum of any two of them has exactly one root.

In a triangle $ABC$ the bisector $CK$ is drawn, and in the triangle $BCK$ the bisector $KL$. The lines $AC$ and $KL$ meet at a point $M$. It is known that $\angle BAC>\angle BCA$. Prove that $AK+KC>AM$.

The numbers from $1$ to $64$ are placed in an $8\times 8$ square. In every row the numbers decrease (from left to right) and in every column the numbers decrease (from top to bottom). Prove that the sum of the $8$ numbers on the diagonal going from the lower left corner to the upper right corner is at least $204$.
How many natural numbers $n$ are there such that when $1\,000\,000$ is divided by $n$, the incomplete quotient is greater than the remainder?

Non-intersecting circles $S_1$ and $S_2$ and their common external tangents $l_1$ and $l_2$ are given. A point $A$ is marked on $l_1$ between the points of tangency, and points $B$ and $C$ are marked on $l_2$ so that $AB$ and $AC$ are tangent to $S_1$ and $S_2$. Let $O_1$ and $O_2$ be the centres of the circles $S_1$ and $S_2$, and let $K$ be the point of tangency of the excircle of the triangle $ABC$ with the side $BC$. Prove that the midpoint of the segment $O_1O_2$ is equidistant from the points $A$ and $K$.

The Thrice-Ninth Kingdom has $2005$ cities. Some cities are connected by one-way roads. It is known that for any two cities one can get from one of them to the other without breaking the traffic rules (that is, for cities $A$ and $B$ one can drive either from $A$ to $B$ or from $B$ to $A$). The king wants to send his governors to several cities so that every city without a governor can be reached directly from a city with a governor. Prove that $1003$ governors will suffice for this.
Let $a$, $b$, $c$ be natural numbers not exceeding $1\,000\,000$. Prove that the equation $$\sqrt[21]{ax^2}+\sqrt[21]{bx}+\sqrt[21]{c}=0$$ has no real solutions.

$10$ distinct numbers are written in a row. One may swap two neighbouring numbers if they have not been swapped before. Prove that if fewer than $45$ such operations have been made, then one more can be made.

A circle passing through the vertices $A$ and $B$ of a triangle $ABC$ meets the sides $AC$ and $BC$ at points $X$ and $Y$ respectively. It turned out that the centre of the excircle of $\triangle CXY$ touching the side $XY$ lies on the circumscribed circle of $\triangle ABC$. Prove that the centre of the inscribed circle of $\triangle ABC$ lies on the segment $XY$.

Can all natural numbers greater than $2005$ be divided into $2$ infinite groups so that the following condition holds: if distinct numbers $x$ and $y$ lie in one group, then the number $x^2+y$ lies in the same group?
Prove the inequality $$(x+1)(y+1)(z+1)\geqslant\sqrt{8(x+y)(x+z)(y+z)}$$ for arbitrary real numbers $x,y,z\in[0,1]$.

Consider all possible sets containing $3$ distinct natural numbers from $1$ to $p-1$, where $p$ is a prime number. For each such set consider the remainder of the product of its numbers upon division by $p$. Prove that among the remainders obtained there are at least as many ones as twos.

Let $BL$ be a bisector of a triangle $ABC$. Inside the triangle $BLC$ there is a point $P$ such that $\angle BPC=90^\circ$ and $\angle LPC+\angle LBC=180^\circ$. The point $O$ is the centre of the circumscribed circle of the triangle $LPB$. Prove that the lines $CO$, $BL$ and $AM$, where $M$ is the midpoint of the side $BC$, meet at one point.

A country has $210$ cities and no roads at all. The king wants to build several one-way roads so that for any three cities $A$, $B$ and $C$ such that there are roads leading from $A$ to $B$ and from $B$ to $C$, there is no road leading from $A$ to $C$. What is the largest number of roads he can build?
A quadratic trinomial $f(x)$ and a geometric progression $q_1, q_2, q_3, q_4$ all of whose terms are distinct are given. Can it happen that $f(q_1)=q_2$, $f(q_2)=q_3$ and $f(q_3)=q_4$?

In an acute-angled triangle $ABC$ the altitudes $AA_1$ and $BB_1$ are drawn. The bisector of the angle $ACB$ meets these altitudes at points $F$ and $L$. Prove that the midpoint of the segment $FL$ is equidistant from the points $A_1$ and $B_1$.

A natural number is written on each of $2006$ cards. Initially all the numbers are coprime as a whole (have no common divisor greater than $1$) and are greater than one (but there may be equal ones among them). Every minute a card with the largest number is chosen (if the largest number is written on several cards, one of them is chosen), its smallest prime divisor is computed, and this divisor is added to the numbers on several other cards. Prove that the numbers on all $2006$ cards cannot become equal.

Kostya cuts a $70\times 70$ square of cells into pieces. Every minute he takes the largest by area of the existing pieces of the square (if there are several such pieces, Kostya may take any of them) and cuts this piece into two by a straight cut along a grid line. Prove that after an hour the areas of all the pieces will be less than a third of the area of the original square.

A point $D$ is marked on the side $AC$ of a triangle $ABC$. An arbitrary ray $\ell$ issuing from the vertex $B$ meets the segment $AC$ at a point $K$ and the circumscribed circle of the triangle $ABC$ at a point $L$. Prove that the circumscribed circle of the triangle $DKL$ passes through a fixed point different from $D$ and not depending on the choice of the ray $\ell$.

There are $2007$ countries and more than $2007$ cities on Mars. Exactly $2006$ roads issue from every Martian city, connecting this city with cities of all the other countries. It is known that from any city one can get by roads to any other city. Prove that there exists a closed route passing (once each) through at least $4012$ cities.

Two irreducible fractions $\frac pq$ and $\frac mn$ were written in decimal notation. Among the places after the decimal point with numbers from $500\,000$ to $1\,000\,000$ there turned out to be fewer than $5\,000$ places in which the digits of these fractions differ, but there is at least one such place. Prove that the denominator of one of these fractions is greater than $10^{50}$.

$101$ natural numbers are written on the board. It is known that the product of any $51$ of these numbers is divisible by the product of the remaining ones. Prove that if the numbers of the set are coprime as a whole, then the product of all the numbers is a power of a natural number.

The point $I$ is the centre of the inscribed circle of a triangle $ABC$. Inside the triangle $ABC$ lies a circle touching the sides $AB$ and $BC$ at points $X$ and $Y$ respectively and meeting the circumscribed circle of the triangle $AIC$ at a point $Z$. Prove that the circumscribed circles of the triangles $AXZ$ and $CYZ$ are tangent to each other.

The quadratic trinomial $2005x^2+2006x+2007$ is given. Two players move alternately. In his move a player may subtract $x^2$, $x$ or $1$ from the polynomial. The player after whose move a polynomial with an integer root is obtained loses. Who wins with correct play: the first player or his opponent?
Solve in natural numbers the equation $n^3-5n+10=2^k$.
problems.proposer: I. Andreeva, N. Kushpel, F. Bakharev, F. Petrov

problems.problem: Let $BL$ be a bisector of an acute-angled triangle $ABC$, let $H$ be its orthocentre, and let the point $K$ be symmetric to the point $L$ with respect to the centre of the circumscribed circle of the triangle $ABC$. Prove that $BK>HL$.

A graph has $n>300$ vertices. In every set $A$ containing at least three vertices of this graph one can point out three vertices each of which is adjacent to at most $200$ vertices of $A$. What is the largest possible number of edges in this graph?

Let $a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n$ be positive numbers the sum of whose squares equals $1$. Prove the inequality $$\sum_{i=1}^n\frac{a_ia_{i+1}}{2-(a_i-a_{i+1})^2}\leqslant\frac12$$ (the numbering of the variables is cyclic, i.e. $a_{n+1}=a_1$).
An odd number $n$ equals the product of three distinct prime numbers. Prove that for any distinct natural numbers $a$ and $b$ the number $a^n-b^n$ has a prime divisor greater than $n$.
problems.proposer: special case of a result of Birkhoff

problems.problem: A quadratic trinomial $f(x)=x^2+px+q$ is such that the equation $f(f(x))=0$ has exactly one root. Prove that the coefficients $p$ and $q$ are non-negative.

$AA_1$ and $CC_1$ are altitudes of an acute-angled triangle $ABC$ in which $\angle ABC=45^\circ$. The points $O$ and $H$ are respectively the circumcentre and the orthocentre of $\triangle ABC$. Prove that the line $A_1C_1$ passes through the midpoint of the segment $OH$.
The decimal representation of the square of a natural number consists of one two and $k-1$ ones written in some order. Prove that $k$ is not divisible by $11$.

For his birthday Baron Munchausen was given a jigsaw puzzle with very many pieces of the five shapes shown in the figure. The baron claims that he has assembled a rectangle from $2006$ such pieces, and all the straight sides of the pieces turned out to be on the boundary of the rectangle. Is the baron mistaken? (The pieces may be rotated and turned over. There must be no gaps inside the rectangle and no overlapping of pieces.)
