$ABCD$ is a convex quadrilateral such that $AD=BD=AC$. The points $M$ and $N$ are the midpoints of the sides $AB$ and $CD$ respectively. The segment $MN$ meets the diagonals of the quadrilateral at points $X$ and $Y$, and $P$ is the intersection point of $AN$ and $DM$. Prove that $PX=PY$.

The numbers $1, 2, 3, \ldots, 2007$ are written on the board in a row. One may choose several of the numbers in this row and replace each of these numbers by their arithmetic mean. Several such operations have been performed. Prove that the number standing after this in the place of the one is less than $2006\frac14$.

A country $A$ has $n\geqslant 3$ cities connected by roads so that one can drive from any city to any other. If any set of roads forming a circular route is closed for repair, then there is a pair of cities between which one cannot travel along the remaining roads. What is the largest possible number of roads in $A$?

Formulation in the language of graphs. A connected graph has $n\geqslant 3$ vertices. After deleting all edges of any cycle the graph becomes disconnected. What is the largest possible number of edges in such a graph?
A $2007\times 2007$ square of cells is divided into $1\times 1$ and $2\times 2$ squares. Prove that there is a row of the original square that meets an odd number of squares of the division.
Distinct natural numbers $a$, $b$ and $c$ satisfy the condition $(a+b)(a+c)=(b+c)^2$. Prove that $(b-c)^2>4(b+c)$.

The line passing through the intersection point of the diagonals of a trapezoid $ABCD$ parallel to the bases $BC$ and $AD$ meets the side $CD$ at a point $K$. A circle passes through the vertices $A$ and $B$ of the trapezoid, meets its bases $BC$ and $AD$ at points $X$ and $Y$ respectively, and touches its side $CD$ at the point $K$. Prove that the line $XY$ passes through the intersection point of the lines $AB$ and $CD$.

Lyosha has $2n$ coins ($n>1$), more than half of which are genuine. It is known that all genuine coins weigh the same, while the weight of any counterfeit coin differs from the weight of a genuine one (but different counterfeit coins may have different weights). Prove that with $2n-3$ weighings on a balance scale without weights Lyosha can find at least one genuine coin.

The trinomial $x^2+25x+425$ is written on the board. Two players play: in one move one may subtract one either from the coefficient of $x$ or from the constant term. The player after whose move a trinomial having a real root is obtained for the first time wins. Who wins with correct play?
$ABCD$ is a cyclic quadrilateral such that $BC=CD$. The point $E$ is the midpoint of the diagonal $AC$. Prove that $BE+DE\geqslant AC$.

Consider an arrangement $a_1$, $a_2$, $\ldots$, $a_{200}$ of the numbers $1$ and $-1$ around a circle. Let $A$ be the number of sign changes when going around the whole circle. Find the sum of the numbers $2^A\cdot a_1\cdots a_{200}$ over all possible arrangements.
Solve in natural numbers the equation $1^n+2^n+\ldots+n^n=k!$.
The graph of $y=x^2+ax+b$ meets the coordinate axes at three distinct points $A$, $B$, $C$. The centre of the circumscribed circle of the triangle $ABC$ lies on the line $y=x$. Prove that $a+b+1=0$.

In a kingdom two-way roads are opened between some cities so that one can drive along the roads from any city to any other. Travel along the roads is paid, and all roads have different costs. The minister compiled a list of all possible routes along the roads of the country passing through every city exactly once. The reforming king marked the most expensive road in each of these routes and ordered all roads marked at least once to be closed. After that it turned out that one cannot drive from city $A$ to city $B$, from city $B$ to city $C$, or from city $C$ to city $A$. Prove that the king's order was carried out incorrectly.
A pentagon $ABCDE$ is circumscribed about a circle $S$. The side $BC$ touches $S$ at a point $K$. It is known that $AB=BC=CD$. Prove that $\angle EKB=90^\circ$.
Numbers $x_1$, $\ldots$, $x_{100}$ are written on the board such that $x_1=1/2$ and for every $n$ from $1$ to $99$ the equality $x_{n+1}=1-x_1x_2\cdots x_n$ holds. Prove that $x_{100}>0.99$.
Distinct natural numbers $a$, $b$, $c$ are given. Prove the inequality $$\gcd(ab+1,\ bc+1,\ ac+1)\leqslant\frac{a+b+c}{3}.$$

A cyclic quadrilateral $ABCD$ is given. The rays $AB$ and $DC$ meet at a point $E$, and the segments $AC$ and $BD$ at a point $F$. Choose a point $P$ on the ray $EF$ such that $\angle BPE=\angle CPE$. Prove that $\angle APB=\angle DPC$.

A $2008\times 2008$ square is divided into regions, each of which is a $1\times 1$ small square. The number $0$ or $1$ is written in each region, and there are equally many zeros and ones in the square. One may erase the boundary between two neighbouring regions, merging them into one; then the numbers written in these regions are removed, and their arithmetic mean is written in the resulting region. After several such operations one region remains, coinciding with the whole square. Prove that the operations can be performed so that the number written in this region is less than $1/2^{10^6}$.
A polynomial of degree three with integer coefficients has three positive irrational roots. Prove that they cannot form a geometric progression.

Several schoolchildren gathered at a party, and each participant of the party had an acquaintance among those present. Moreover, each of those present had exactly $3.2$ times as many acquaintances among the boys as among the girls. What is the smallest number of schoolchildren that could have gathered at the party?
Denote by $p(a)$ the smallest prime divisor of a natural number $a>1$. For natural numbers $m,n>1$ the relation $$m+n=(p(m)-p(n))(p(m)+p(n))$$ holds. What values can the number $m$ take?

A cyclic quadrilateral $ABCD$ is given. Let $s_1$ be the circle passing through $A$ and $B$ and tangent to the line $AC$, and let $s_2$ be the circle passing through $C$ and $D$ and tangent to $AC$. Prove that the lines $AC$, $BD$ and the second common internal tangent of $s_1$ and $s_2$ pass through one point.

A superknight is a chess piece one move of which consists of two steps of an ordinary knight. (In particular, a superknight attacks the cell on which it stands.) Several cells of an infinite board are painted blue. Denote by $N$ the number of cells that can be reached by a knight's move from the blue cells. Prove that one can place at most $N/8$ superknights on the board that together attack all the blue cells.
A trapezoid $ABCD$ $(AB\parallel CD)$ is given. Denote by $R_1$ and $R_2$ the radii of the circumscribed circles of the triangles $ACD$ and $BCD$. Prove that $$AB^2\leqslant 4R_1R_2.$$
Prove that for all natural $a$ and $b$ the inequality $$(ab)^{a^2+b^2}\left(\frac{a^2+b^2}{2}\right)^{2ab}\leqslant\left(\frac{a+b}{2}\right)^{2(a+b)^2}$$ holds.

Two players alternately write a sequence of natural numbers on the board. Initially the sequence consists of three terms: $1, 2, 3$. In one move one may append to the sequence one term equal to the sum of the last written term and one of the earlier ones. The player who obtains a number not less than $1000$ wins. Who wins with correct play?
Natural numbers $b$ and $c$ are given such that $c+1$ is divisible by $b$. Prove that there exist natural numbers $x$, $y$ and $z$ such that $x+y=bz$ and $xy=cz$.

$40$ jury members are choosing the second problem for grade $9$. They have a list of $30$ problems. They agreed to put into the paper a problem that at least half of the jury members can solve, but not all of them. Each jury member solved exactly $26$ problems, and any two jury members solved different sets of problems. Prove that they will be able to find a suitable problem.
Distinct natural numbers $x$, $y$ and $z$ satisfy the condition $$\operatorname{lcm}(x,y)-\operatorname{lcm}(x,z)=y-z.$$ Prove that $y$ and $z$ are divisible by $x$.

Points $A_1$ and $C_1$ are chosen on the sides $BC$ and $AB$ of an acute-angled triangle $ABC$. The segments $AA_1$ and $CC_1$ meet at a point $K$. The circumscribed circles of the triangles $AA_1B$ and $CC_1B$ meet at a point $P$. It turned out that the point $P$ is the centre of the inscribed circle of the triangle $AKC$. Prove that the point $P$ is the orthocentre of the triangle $ABC$.

In an acute-angled triangle $ABC$ the altitudes $AA_1$, $BB_1$ and $CC_1$ are drawn. The points $X$ and $Y$ are the midpoints of the segments $CA_1$ and $AC_1$. It is known that $XY=BB_1$. Prove that the ratio of some two sides of the triangle $ABC$ equals $\sqrt2$.

Call a board an arbitrary set of cells of the grid plane. A set of rooks on a board is called beautiful if they do not attack each other but attack all the other cells of the board. (A rook attacks every cell lying in the same row or the same column as it, even if not all cells between them belong to the board.) Prove that if on some board one can place a beautiful set of $2008$ rooks and one can place a beautiful set of $2010$ rooks, then one can also place a beautiful set of $2009$ rooks.
problems.proposer: K. Kokhas, S. Berlov, F. Petrov et al.

problems.problem: The discriminants of the quadratic trinomials $$f(x),\ g(x),\ h(x),\ f(x)+g(x),\ g(x)+h(x)\ \text{and}\ f(x)+h(x)$$ are equal to $1$. Prove that $f(x)+g(x)+h(x)$ is the zero polynomial.

A king stands on some cell of a chessboard. Every day, starting from Monday, Seryozha makes one move with this king. On Sundays he moves it one cell diagonally, and on each of the other days one cell horizontally or vertically. Seryozha never puts the king on a cell the king has already visited (the initial cell is considered visited). What is the largest number of cells the king can visit?

The points $M$ and $N$ are the midpoints of the sides $AB$ and $CD$ of a convex quadrilateral $ABCD$. Points $X$ and $Y$ are chosen on the sides $AD$ and $BC$ so that $XD=3AX$ and $YC=3BY$. It turned out that $\angle MXA=\angle MYB=90^\circ$. Prove that $\angle XMN=\angle ABC$.
The numbers $a$ and $a^3-6a$ are roots of a quadratic trinomial with integer coefficients. Moreover, the number $a$ is irrational. What can $a$ be equal to?

A natural number $A$ has $20$ digits. The number $\underbrace{AA\ldots A}_{101\text{ times}}$ was written on the board, after which its last $11$ digits were erased. Prove that the resulting $2009$-digit number cannot be a power of two.

A country has $2010$ cities, and any two of them are connected by a road (not passing through other cities). A businessman and the Ministry of Road Construction play a game. Every morning the businessman privatizes one of the roads, and every evening the Ministry destroys ten roads not yet privatized. Can the businessman, despite the Ministry's intrigues, create a cyclic route along privatized roads passing once through each of $11$ different cities?
Positive numbers $a$, $b$, $c$ satisfy the condition $\dfrac{3}{abc}\geqslant a+b+c$. Prove the inequality $\dfrac1a+\dfrac1b+\dfrac1c\geqslant a+b+c$.

The inscribed circle of a triangle $ABC$ touches its sides $BC$, $CA$ and $AB$ at points $A_1$, $B_1$ and $C_1$ respectively. The line $AA_1$ meets this circle a second time at a point $E$. The point $N$ is the midpoint of the segment $A_1B_1$. The point $M$ is symmetric to the point $N$ with respect to the line $AA_1$. Prove that $\angle EMC=90^\circ$.

The teacher gave Dima and Seryozha a quadratic trinomial each, wrote $4$ numbers on the board and told each of the pupils to substitute these four numbers into his quadratic trinomial. Seryozha obtained the values $1$, $3$, $5$ and $7$. Dima managed to substitute only the first three numbers and obtained $17$, $15$ and $13$. When Dima was about to substitute the fourth number, it turned out that the teacher had already erased the numbers from the board. What value would he have obtained if he had managed to substitute the fourth number? (The answer must be a specific number.)
For natural numbers $a$ and $b$ the inequality $$a\cdot\gcd(a,b)+b\cdot\operatorname{lcm}(a,b)<2.5\,ab$$ holds. Prove that $a$ is divisible by $b$.
A point $D$ is chosen inside a triangle $ABC$ such that $AD=DC$. The line $BD$ meets the side $AC$ at a point $E$. It turned out that $\frac{BD}{BE}=\frac{AE}{EC}$. Prove that $BE=BC$.

The town of Ugryumov has $2\,000\,000$ inhabitants who communicate little with each other. Nevertheless, among any $2000$ inhabitants there are three pairwise acquainted. Prove that the town has four inhabitants pairwise acquainted with each other.

In a convex quadrilateral $ABCD$ all angles are less than $150^\circ$, and the sum of the angles $A$ and $D$ equals $150^\circ$. Prove that its area is greater than $\frac14(AB\cdot CD+AB\cdot BC+BC\cdot CD)$.

An infinite sequence $a_1$, $a_2$, $a_3$, $\ldots$ of composite natural numbers is defined by the following rule: $a_{n+1}=a_n-p_n+a_n/p_n$, where $p_n$ is the smallest prime divisor of $a_n$. It is known that all terms of the sequence are multiples of $37$. What values can the number $a_1$ take?

Sasha and Seryozha play a game on a regular $100$-gon. At the beginning of the game Sasha places natural numbers at the vertices of the $100$-gon. Then the players move alternately, Seryozha beginning. In each move Seryozha adds $1$ to the numbers at two opposite vertices, and Sasha adds $1$ to the numbers at two neighbouring vertices. Seryozha strives to have as many odd numbers as possible on the $100$-gon after his move. What is the largest number he can achieve regardless of Sasha's actions?
Find all integers $b$ for which the equation $[x^2]-2012x+b=0$ has an odd number of roots.

Natural numbers $a$, $b$, $c$ are greater than $100$ and coprime as a whole (that is, the three numbers have no common divisor other than $1$). It is known that $a+b$ is divisible by $c$ and $b+c$ is divisible by $a$. Find the smallest possible value of $b$.

The bisector of the angle between the diagonals of a cyclic quadrilateral $ABCD$ meets the sides $AB$ and $CD$ at points $X$ and $Y$ respectively. It is known that the midpoint of the side $AD$ is equidistant from the points $X$ and $Y$. Prove that the midpoint of the side $BC$ is also equidistant from the points $X$ and $Y$.

$25$ schoolchildren take part in the Unified State Exam. The exam consists of several questions, to each of which one of five answer options can be given. It turned out that any two schoolchildren answered at most one question in the same way. Prove that the exam had at most $6$ questions.

Natural numbers are placed in the cells of a $100\times 100$ square, and in every row and every column all numbers are distinct. Can it happen that for every square with sides along the grid lines, the sum of the numbers in the four corner cells of this square is the square of a natural number?

A point $L$ is chosen on the bisector of the angle $B$ of a triangle $ABC$ (inside the triangle), and a point $K$ is chosen on the segment $BL$. It is known that $\angle KAB=\angle LCB=\alpha$. A point $P$ is chosen inside the triangle such that $AP=PC$ and $\angle APC=2\angle AKL$. Prove that $\angle KPL=2\alpha$.

The donkey Eeyore has $2012$ sticks of natural lengths, the sum of their lengths being $n$. The donkey wants to break off from them $2012$ sticks: of length $1$, of length $2$, $\ldots$, of length $2012$. (Several sticks may be broken off from one stick; for example, sticks of lengths $1$ and $4$ can be broken off from a stick of length $6$.) For what smallest $n$ can Eeyore certainly do this?

A natural number $A$ is called interesting if it is divisible by every number that remains after deleting several last digits of $A$. Find the largest interesting number consisting of distinct digits.
The sum of the squares of the real numbers $a$, $b$, $c$ and $d$ equals $1$. Prove that $(1-a)(1-b)\geqslant cd$.

The bisector of the angle $B$ of a triangle $ABC$ meets the line passing through $A$ parallel to $BC$ at a point $X$; it also meets the line passing through $C$ parallel to $AB$ at a point $Y$. It is known that $XY=AC$. By how much can the angles $A$ and $C$ differ?

There are $100$ glasses on a table containing $101, 102, \ldots, 200$ cherry stones. Two players play the following game. In one move one may take out of any glass any number of stones (even all), but after the move all glasses must still contain different numbers of stones. The player who cannot move loses. Who wins with correct play?

$100$ numbers from the interval $(0,1)$ are written on the board. One may choose two numbers $a$ and $b$ and replace them by the two roots of the quadratic trinomial $x^2-ax+b$ (if this trinomial has two roots). Prove that this process cannot continue indefinitely.

The diagonals of a quadrilateral $ABCD$ meet at a point $O$. The points $X$ and $Y$ are symmetric to the point $O$ with respect to the midpoints of the sides $BC$ and $AD$ respectively. It is known that $AB=BC=CD$. Prove that the intersection point of the perpendicular bisectors of the diagonals of the quadrilateral lies on the line $XY$.
A $54$-digit number consisting of ones and zeros is given. Prove that the remainder of its division by the number $33\cdot 34\cdot\ldots\cdot 39$ is greater than $100\,000$.
A quadratic trinomial $f(x)$ swaps distinct numbers $a$ and $b$ (i.e. $f(a)=b$ and $f(b)=a$). Prove that it does not swap any other two numbers.

An acute-angled triangle $ABC$, all of whose angles are greater than $30^\circ$, is inscribed in a circle with centre $O$ and radius $R$. The point $K$ is the projection of $O$ onto the bisector of the angle $B$, and the point $M$ is the midpoint of the side $AC$. It turned out that $2KM=R$. Find the angle $B$.

$100$ deputies formed $450$ commissions. Every two commissions have at most three deputies in common, and every $5$ at most one. Prove that there are four commissions having exactly one deputy in common.

Call a natural number venerable if the sum of all its divisors, including $1$ but not including the number itself, is $1$ less than this number. Find all venerable numbers some exact power of which is also venerable.

A $100\times 100$ napkin is thrown arbitrarily onto the grid plane with unit cell side. It covers some nodes (a node lying on the boundary of the napkin is also considered covered). What is the smallest number of lines (not necessarily along grid lines) with which all these nodes can certainly be covered?

Points $A$ and $B$ are fixed on a given circle. Points $C$ and $D$ move along one of the arcs $AB$ so that the segment $CD$ has constant length. The points $I_1$ and $I_2$ are the centres of the inscribed circles of the triangles $ABC$ and $ABD$. Prove that the line $I_1I_2$ is always tangent to some fixed circle.

Natural numbers $a$, $b$ and $c$ are pairwise coprime. Integers are placed in an infinite grid table so that the sum of the numbers in every $a\times a$ square is even, in every $b\times b$ square is even and in every $c\times c$ square is also even. Is it true that for any $a$, $b$, $c$ such a situation is possible only if all the numbers in the table are even?
Does there exist a quadratic trinomial $f(x)$ with integer coefficients such that $f(f(\sqrt2))=0$?
An isosceles trapezoid $ABCD$ $(AD\parallel BC)$ is given. It is known that $AD>BC$. A point $E$ is marked on its circumscribed circle such that $BE\perp AD$. Prove that $AE+BC>DE$.

The cells of a $2015\times 2015$ square are coloured in $4$ colours. All ways of placing inside this square a four-cell T-shaped piece (three cells in a row and one more cell attached to the middle one; the piece may be rotated) are considered. Prove that the piece contains cells of four different colours in less than $51\%$ of these ways.
Positive numbers $x$, $y$, $z$ satisfy the condition $$xy+yz+zx+2xyz=1.$$ Prove that $4x+y+z\geqslant 2$.

A convex quadrilateral $ABCD$ is given. The circumscribed circle of the triangle $ABC$ meets the sides $AD$ and $DC$ at points $P$ and $Q$ respectively. The circumscribed circle of the triangle $ADC$ meets the sides $AB$ and $BC$ at points $S$ and $R$ respectively. It turned out that the quadrilateral $PQRS$ is a parallelogram. Prove that the quadrilateral $ABCD$ is also a parallelogram.

An intergalactic empire has $10^{2015}$ planets, any two of which are connected by a two-way direct space line. These lines are owned by $2015$ transport companies. The emperor wants to close $k$ companies so that, using only the flights of the remaining ones, one can still get from any planet to any other. For what largest $k$ can he certainly carry out his plan?

A sequence of natural numbers is defined as follows: $a_1=1$, $a_2=2$, $a_3=3$, and $a_n$ is the smallest natural number that has not occurred before, is coprime to $a_{n-1}$ and is not coprime to $a_{n-2}$. Prove that every natural number occurs in this sequence exactly once.

Three quadratic trinomials $f$, $g$, $h$ having no roots are given. Their leading coefficients are equal, and all their coefficients of $x$ are different. Prove that there exists a number $c$ such that the equations $$f(x)+cg(x)=0\qquad\text{and}\qquad f(x)+ch(x)=0$$ have a common root.

Several rooks are placed on a $300\times 300$ board so that they attack the whole board. Moreover, each rook attacks at most one other rook. For what smallest $k$ can one assert for certain that every $k\times k$ square contains at least one rook?

Points $P$ and $Q$ are chosen on the side $AB$ of a non-isosceles triangle $ABC$ so that $AC=AP$ and $BC=BQ$. The perpendicular bisector of the segment $PQ$ meets the bisector of the angle $C$ at a point $R$ (inside the triangle). Prove that $$\angle ACB+\angle PRQ=180^\circ.$$

Two distinct prime numbers $p$ and $q$ differ by less than a factor of two. Prove that there exist two consecutive natural numbers such that the largest prime divisor of one of them equals $p$, and that of the other equals $q$.

Kostya and Sergei play a game on a white strip of length $2016$. Kostya (who moves first) must paint black two neighbouring white cells in one move. Sergei in his move must paint either one white cell or three neighbouring white cells. It is forbidden to make a move after which a white cell having no white neighbours appears. The player who cannot move loses. However, if all cells are painted, Kostya wins. Who wins with correct play?

The inscribed circle of a triangle $ABC$ touches the side $AC$ at a point $D$. The segment $BD$ meets the circle again at a point $E$. Points $F$ and $G$ on the circle are such that $FE\parallel BC$ and $GE\parallel BA$. Prove that the segment joining the centres of the inscribed circles of the triangles $DEF$ and $DEG$ is bisected by the bisector of the angle $GDF$.
A block of $N$ consecutive natural numbers is called good if the product of some two of them is divisible by the sum of the others. For which $N$ are there infinitely many good blocks?

Sasha's computer can perform two operations. If a card with the number $a$ is loaded into it, it returns the card and prints one more card with the number $a+1$. If cards with the numbers $a$ and $b$ are loaded into it one after the other, it returns them and prints cards with all the roots of the quadratic trinomial $x^2+ax+b$ (one, two, or none). Initially Sasha had only a card with the number $s$. Is it true that for every $s>0$ Sasha can at some moment obtain a card with the number $\sqrt s$?

In a triangle $ABC$ there is a point $X$ on the side $AB$ such that $2BX=BA+BC$. The point $Y$ is symmetric to the centre $I$ of the inscribed circle of the triangle $ABC$ with respect to the point $X$. Prove that $YI_B$ is perpendicular to $AB$, where $I_B$ is the centre of the excircle of the triangle $ABC$ touching the side $AC$.

Petya, Vasya and Tolya play the following game on a $100\times 100$ board. They take turns (Petya begins, then Vasya, then Tolya, then Petya again, and so on) painting boundary cells of the board (i.e. cells having a common side with the boundary of the board). It is forbidden to paint a cell adjacent by a side to an already painted cell. Moreover, it is forbidden to paint a cell symmetric to an already painted cell with respect to the centre of the board. The player who cannot move loses. Can Vasya and Tolya, by agreement, play so that Petya loses?

Natural numbers are written in the cells of a $3\times n$ table. Each of the three rows contains each of the numbers $1, 2, \ldots, n$ exactly once. For each column, the sum of the pairwise products of the three numbers standing in it is a multiple of $n$. For which $n$ is this possible?

In a non-isosceles triangle $ABC$ the angle $B$ equals $130^\circ$. The point $H$ is the foot of the altitude from the vertex $B$. On the sides $AB$ and $BC$ there are points $D$ and $E$ respectively such that $DH=EH$ and the quadrilateral $ADEC$ is cyclic. Find the angle $DHE$.

The numbers $a$, $b$ and $c$ lie in the interval $[0,1)$ and satisfy the relation $a^2+b^2+c^2=1$. What is the smallest value that the quantity $$\frac{a}{\sqrt{1-a^2}}+\frac{b}{\sqrt{1-b^2}}+\frac{c}{\sqrt{1-c^2}}$$ can take?

Call a grid quadrant the quarter of the plane lying above the $X$ axis and to the right of the $Y$ axis, divided into unit cells. $n^2$ cells are painted in the grid quadrant. Prove that in this quadrant there are at least $n^2+n$ cells (including painted ones) adjacent by a side to at least one painted cell.

Prove that for every natural number $N$ there exists an integer $k\geqslant 0$ such that $N$ can be written as a sum of the numbers $2^0$, $2^1$, $2^2$, $\ldots$, $2^k$, each of which occurs in this sum once or twice. (For example, $12=2^0+2^0+2^1+2^2+2^2$.)

An odd natural number $n>1$ is given. The numbers $n$, $n+1$, $n+2$, $\ldots$, $2n-1$ are written on the board. Prove that one can erase one of them so that the sum of the remaining numbers is not divisible by any of the remaining numbers.

An acute-angled triangle $ABC$ is given. Variable points $X$ and $Y$ are chosen on the segment $AC$ and on the extension of the side $BC$ beyond the point $C$ respectively in such a way that $\angle ABX+\angle CXY=90^\circ$. The point $T$ is the projection of the point $B$ onto the line $XY$. Prove that all such points $T$ lie on one line.

$n>3$ beads hang on a circular necklace, each coloured red or blue. If both neighbours of some bead are coloured the same, it may be recoloured (from red to blue or from blue to red). For which $n$ can one obtain, from any initial colouring of the beads, a necklace in which all beads are coloured the same?
Can one draw a triangle $ABC$ in the plane and mark two points $X$ and $Y$ in the same plane so that $AX=BY=AB$, $BX=CY=BC$, $CX=AY=CA$?
Two odd natural numbers $a$ and $b$ are given. Prove that there exists a natural number $k$ such that at least one of the numbers $b^k-a^2$ and $a^k-b^2$ is divisible by $2^{2018}$.

In a $10\times 10$ grid square (the sides of the cells have unit length), $n$ cells were chosen; in each of them one of the diagonals was drawn and an arrow was put on this diagonal in one of the two directions. It turned out that for any two arrows either the end of one of them coincides with the beginning of the other, or the distance between their ends is at least $2$. For what largest $n$ is this possible?

A natural number is called a palindrome if it reads the same from left to right and from right to left (in particular, the last digit of a palindrome coincides with the first and is therefore not zero). The squares of two distinct natural numbers have $1001$ digits each. Prove that strictly between these squares on the number line there is a palindrome.

$2019$ metro stations have been built in a city. Some pairs of stations are connected by tunnels, and one can get from any station to any other through tunnels. The mayor ordered several metro lines to be organized: each line must include several distinct stations successively connected by tunnels (several lines may pass through the same tunnel). Every station must lie on at least one line. To save money, at most $k$ lines are to be made. It turned out that the mayor's order cannot be carried out. For what largest $k$ could this have happened?
Prove that the distance between the midpoint of the side $BC$ of a triangle $ABC$ and the midpoint of the arc $ABC$ of its circumscribed circle is not less than $AB/2$.

Olya wrote on cards the fractions of the form $1/n$, where $n$ runs over all possible divisors of the number $6^{100}$ (including one and the number itself). She laid out these cards in some order. Then she wrote on the board the number on the first card, then the sum of the numbers on the first and second cards, then the sum of the numbers on the first three cards, and so on, and finally the sum of the numbers on all the cards. Olya wrote each sum on the board as an irreducible fraction. What is the smallest possible number of distinct denominators among the numbers on the board?

An improvement of a positive number is its replacement by a power of two (i.e. by one of the numbers $1, 2, 4, 8, \ldots$) under which it increases, but by at most a factor of $3$. $2^{100}$ positive numbers with sum $2^{100}$ are given. Prove that one can erase some of them and improve each of the remaining numbers so that the sum of the resulting numbers is again equal to $2^{100}$.

The bisectors $BB_1$ and $CC_1$ of an acute-angled triangle $ABC$ meet at a point $I$. Points $B'$ and $C'$ are marked on the extensions of the segments $BB_1$ and $CC_1$ respectively so that the quadrilateral $AB'IC'$ is a parallelogram. Prove that if $\angle BAC=60^\circ$, then the line $B'C'$ passes through the intersection point of the circumscribed circles of the triangles $BC_1B'$ and $CB_1C'$.

$2019$ saucers are arranged around a circle, and there is one cake on each. Petya and Vasya play a game. In one move Petya points to a cake and names a number from $1$ to $16$, and Vasya moves the indicated cake by the indicated number of saucers clockwise or counterclockwise (Vasya chooses the direction each time). Petya wants at some moment at least $k$ cakes to accumulate on one of the saucers, and Vasya wants to prevent him. For what largest $k$ can Petya succeed?

What is the largest number of solutions the equation $$\max\{a_1x+b_1,\ldots,a_{10}x+b_{10}\}=0$$ can have, if $a_1$, $\ldots$, $a_{10}$, $b_1$, $\ldots$, $b_{10}$ are real numbers and all $a_i$ are non-zero?

Call a triple of natural numbers $a$, $b$, $c$ interesting if $(a^2+1)(b^2+1)$ is a multiple of $c^2+1$, but neither of the two factors is itself a multiple of $c^2+1$. An interesting triple $a$, $b$, $c$ is given. Prove that there exist natural numbers $u$, $v$ for which the triple $u$, $v$, $c$ is interesting and $uv<c^3$.
A point $E$ is marked on the side $AD$ of a convex quadrilateral $ABCD$ with an acute angle $B$. It is known that $\angle CAD=\angle ADC=\angle ABE=\angle DBE$. Prove that $BE+CE<AD$.

A table has $25$ columns and $300$ rows; Kostya coloured all its cells in three colours. Then Lyosha, looking at the table, names one of the three colours for each row and marks all cells of this colour in this row. (If there are no cells of the named colour in the row, he marks nothing in it.) After that all columns containing at least one marked cell are crossed out of the table. Kostya wants as few columns as possible to remain in the table, and Lyosha wants as many as possible. What is the largest number of columns Lyosha can guarantee to leave?

The point $I_a$ is the centre of the excircle of a triangle $ABC$ touching the side $BC$ at a point $X$, and the point $A'$ is diametrically opposite to the point $A$ on the circumscribed circle of this triangle. Points $Y$, $Z$, $T$ are chosen on the segments $I_aX$, $BA'$, $CA'$ respectively so that $I_aY=BZ=CT=r$, where $r$ is the radius of the inscribed circle of the triangle $ABC$. Prove that the points $X$, $Y$, $Z$, $T$ lie on one circle.

The following points are marked in the coordinate plane: $(1,1)$, $(2,3)$, $(4,5)$, $(999,111)$. If a point $(a,b)$ is marked, then one may also mark the points $(b,a)$ and $(a-b,a+b)$; if points $(a,b)$ and $(c,d)$ are marked, then one may mark the point $(ad+bc,4ac-4bd)$. Will it be possible sooner or later to mark a point on the line $y=2x$?

A graph has $400$ vertices. For any edge $AB$, call the set of all edges issuing from the vertices $A$ and $B$ (including the edge $AB$ itself) a cuttlefish. Each edge of the graph carries the number $1$ or $-1$. It is known that the sum of the numbers on the edges of any cuttlefish is at least $1$. Prove that the sum of the numbers on all edges of the graph is not less than $-10000$.

$2021$ points are placed on a circle. Kostya marks a point, then marks the neighbouring point to the right, then the point to the right skipping one from the one just marked, then the point to the right skipping two from the one just marked, and so on. On which move will a point marked twice appear for the first time?

Misha has a $100\times 100$ chessboard and a bag with $199$ rooks. In one move one may either put one rook from the bag on the lower left cell, or take two rooks standing on the same cell, put one of them on the cell adjacent to it from above or from the right, and put the other into the bag. Misha wants to place $100$ rooks on the board not attacking each other. Can he obtain any such arrangement?
In a cyclic quadrilateral $ABCD$, $\angle A=3\angle B$. A point $C_1$ is marked on the side $AB$, and a point $A_1$ on the side $BC$, so that $AA_1=AC=CC_1$. Prove that $3A_1C_1>BD$.

$n$ points with different abscissas are marked in the plane. Through every pair of points a parabola is drawn, i.e. the graph of a quadratic trinomial with leading coefficient one. A parabola is called good if there are no marked points on it or above it except the two through which it is drawn. What is the largest possible number of good parabolas?

An isosceles trapezoid $ABCD$, in which the base $AD$ is twice the lateral side $AB$, is inscribed in a circle $\omega$. Points $E$ and $F$ are chosen on the circle $\omega$ so that $AC\parallel DE$ and $BD\parallel AF$. The segment $BE$ meets the segments $AC$ and $AF$ at points $X$ and $Y$ respectively. Prove that the circumscribed circles of the triangles $BCX$ and $EFY$ are tangent.

A school has $450$ pupils. Each of them has at least $100$ friends among the others, and among any $200$ pupils there are always two friends. Prove that one can send $302$ pupils on a canoe trip so that in each of the $151$ two-seat canoes there are friends.
A natural number $n$ is given. For every prime number $p$ in the interval $[n,n^4]$ the number $\frac1p$ was computed, and all the numbers obtained were added. Prove that their sum is less than $4$.
Natural numbers $a$ and $b$ are such that $a+k$ is divisible by $b+k$ for all natural $k<b$. Prove that $a-k$ is divisible by $b-k$ for all natural $k<b$.

$12$ schoolchildren attend a patriotic song club; each of them knows several songs (possibly none). We say that a group of schoolchildren can sing a song if at least one member of the group knows it. The head of the club noticed that any group of $10$ club members can sing exactly $20$ songs, and any group of $8$ club members exactly $16$ songs. Prove that the group of all $12$ club members can sing exactly $24$ songs.

Prove that the intersection points of the bisectors of opposite angles of a trapezoid, together with the endpoints of either of its bases, lie on one circle. For definiteness, assume that the points are positioned as shown in the figure.

We say that a point $(u,v)$ of the plane lies between the parabolas $y=f(x)$ and $y=g(x)$ if $f(u)\leqslant v\leqslant g(u)$. Find the smallest real $p$ for which the following statement holds: every segment whose endpoints and midpoint lie between the parabolas $y=x^2$ and $y=x^2+1$ lies entirely between the parabolas $y=x^2$ and $y=x^2+p$.

There are two piles of stones: $1703$ stones in one pile and $2022$ in the other. Sasha and Olya play a game, moving alternately; Sasha begins. Suppose that before a player's move the piles contain $a$ and $b$ stones, where $a\geqslant b$. Then in his move the player may take from the pile with $a$ stones any number of stones from $1$ to $b$. The player who cannot move loses. Who wins with correct play?

In a triangle $ABC$ the median $BM$ is drawn. On the tangent at the point $C$ to the circumscribed circle of the triangle $BMC$ a point $D$ is marked such that $\angle CBD=90^\circ$. The segments $AD$ and $BM$ meet at a point $E$. Prove that the centre of the circumscribed circle of the triangle $BDE$ lies on the line $AC$.

$n$ distinct natural numbers are given, any two of which are obtained from each other by a permutation of digits (zero cannot be put in the first place). For what largest $n$ can all these numbers be divisible by the smallest of them?
Real numbers $a$ and $b$ greater than $1$ satisfy the inequality $$a+\frac{1}{a^2}\geqslant 5b-\frac{3}{b^2}.$$ Prove that $a>5b-\dfrac{4}{b^2}$.

Several (at least $5$) integers are placed around a circle so that each of them is divisible by the sum of its two neighbours. The sum of all the numbers is positive. What is the smallest value it can take?

The point $M$ is the midpoint of the side $AC$ of an acute-angled triangle $ABC$. A point $K$ is chosen on the minor arc $AC$ of the circumscribed circle of this triangle so that the angle $AKM$ is a right angle. The segments $BK$ and $AM$ meet at a point $X$, and the altitude drawn from the vertex $A$ meets the segment $BM$ at a point $Y$. Prove that the lines $XY$ and $AB$ are parallel.

One side of a square sheet of paper is painted red, the other blue. On both sides the sheet is divided into $300^2$ equal square cells. A number from $1$ to $k$ is written in each of these $2\cdot 300^2$ cells. Find the smallest $k$ for which the following properties can hold simultaneously: (i) on the red side any two numbers standing in different rows are different; (ii) on the blue side any two numbers standing in different columns are different; (iii) for each of the $300^2$ squares of the division, the number on the blue side is not equal to the number on the red side.

For a natural number $n$ and a non-zero digit $d$, denote by $f(n,d)$ the smallest natural $k$ for which the number $kn$ begins with the digit $d$. What is the largest value the quantity $f(n,d)$ can take?

Baron Munchausen said jokingly that he had placed $2\,000\,000$ rabbits in $1\,000\,000$ cages so that each cage contains at most one rabbit. The burgomaster took these words seriously and asks the baron questions of the form "is it true that such-and-such rabbit sits in such-and-such cage". The burgomaster believes that he will catch the baron lying in one of three cases: 1) if the baron answers "yes" to questions about the same rabbit and two different cages; 2) if the baron answers "yes" to questions about the same cage and two different rabbits; 3) if the baron answers "no" to the questions about some rabbit and all the existing cages. Can the baron answer so that the burgomaster cannot catch him lying by asking $10^{11}$ questions?

A triangle $ABC$ is given. The point $X$ is symmetric to the vertex $B$ with respect to the line $AC$, and the point $Y$ is symmetric to $C$ with respect to the line $AB$. The tangent to the circumscribed circle of the triangle $XAY$ drawn at the point $A$ meets the lines $XY$ and $BC$ at points $E$ and $F$ respectively. Prove that $AE=AF$.

Dima has a red and a blue felt-tip pen; with one of them he colours rational points of the number line, and with the other irrational ones. Dima coloured $100$ rational and $100$ irrational points, after which he erased the labels that made it possible to find out where the origin was and what the scale was. Sergei has a pair of compasses with which he can measure the distance between any two coloured points $A$ and $B$ and then mark on the line a point at the measured distance from any coloured point $C$ (to the left or to the right); Dima immediately colours it with the corresponding pen. How can Sergei find out which colour Dima uses for rational points and which for irrational ones?

The strongman Bambula can carry several weights at once if their total weight does not exceed $200$ kg and there are at most three of them. On the way to work he injured a finger and found that now he can carry at most two weights (and still at most $200$ kg). For what smallest $k$ is the following statement true: any set of $100$ weights that Bambula could previously carry in $50$ trips he can carry with the injured finger in at most $k$ trips?

A triangle $ABC$ is inscribed in a circle. Two ants simultaneously crawl out of the points $B$ and $C$. They crawl along the arc $BC$ towards each other so that the product of their distances to the point $A$ remains constant. Prove that during their motion (until the moment they meet) the line passing through the ants is tangent to some fixed circle.

A coach lined up $200$ volleyball players in a row and handed out $m$ balls to them (each player could receive any number of balls). From time to time one of the players throws a ball to another (who catches it). After some time it turned out that for any two players, the left one threw a ball to the right one exactly twice, and the right one to the left one exactly once. For what smallest $m$ is this possible?

$AH$ is an altitude of an acute-angled triangle $ABC$ inscribed in a circle $s$. Points $D$ and $E$ were chosen on the segment $BH$. Points $X$ and $Y$ were chosen on the rays $AD$ and $AE$ respectively so that the midpoints of the segments $DX$ and $EY$ lie on the circle $s$. It turned out that the points $B$, $X$, $Y$ and $C$ lie on one circle. Prove that $BD+BE=2CH$.

Call a natural number $n$ poor if the equation $$x_1x_2\cdots x_{101}=(n-x_1)(n-x_2)\cdots(n-x_{101})$$ has no solutions in natural numbers $1<x_i<n$. Does there exist a poor number having more than $100\,000$ distinct prime divisors?

A metro is being built in a very large City: many stations, some pairs of which are connected by tunnels, and one can get from any station to any other through tunnels. All tunnels of the metro must be divided into "lines": each line consists of several consecutive tunnels, all of whose stations are distinct (in particular, a line must not be circular); lines consisting of a single tunnel are allowed. The law requires that one can travel from any station to any other making at most $100$ changes from line to line. For what largest $N$ can every connected metro with $N$ stations be divided into lines in accordance with the law?

Call semiprime the natural numbers equal to the product of two distinct prime numbers. Let $a<b<c<d$ be four consecutive semiprime numbers. It turned out that there is a square of a prime number between the numbers $a$ and $b$, and also a square of a prime number between the numbers $c$ and $d$. Prove that there are no squares of prime numbers between the numbers $b$ and $c$.

A convex quadrilateral $ABCD$ is given in which $AB=BC=CD\neq AD$. The bisectors of the angles $A$ and $C$ meet inside the quadrilateral. Prove that the bisectors of the angles $B$ and $D$ cannot meet inside the quadrilateral.

For what largest $n$ can one mark some cells of a $100\times 100$ chessboard so that there are two marked cells $A$ and $B$ such that a chess king, moving along marked cells, can get from $A$ to $B$ in $n$ moves, but cannot do it in fewer than $n$ moves?

Positive numbers $a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n$ are such that $a_1^2+\ldots+a_n^2=1$. Prove the inequality $$\frac{1}{a_1-a_1^3}+\frac{1}{a_2-a_2^3}+\ldots+\frac{1}{a_n-a_n^3}\geqslant\left(a_1+a_2+\ldots+a_n\right)\left(\frac{1}{1-a_1^2}+\frac{1}{1-a_2^2}+\ldots+\frac{1}{1-a_n^2}\right).$$

Berries grow on several bushes. Every day from the 1st to the 30th of July the berries grow according to the following rule. If the weather on the $k$-th of July is good, then exactly at noon one new berry grows on every bush having fewer than $k$ berries (on the other bushes the number of berries does not change). If the weather is bad, then at noon one berry grows on every bush having at least $k$ berries. On the evening of the 30th of July it turned out that the numbers of berries on the bushes are different and do not exceed $30$. Find the largest possible number of bushes.
Natural numbers $a$, $b$, $c$ and $n$ are such that $a^2-nab+b^2=c^2$. Prove that the number $a+b+(n+1)c$ is composite.

In a triangle $ABC$ the median $AM$ and the bisector $AL$ are drawn. The altitude drawn to the side $BC$ meets the inscribed circle at points $X$ and $Y$, and the extension of this altitude meets one of the excircles at points $Z$ and $T$. Prove that $\angle XLY=\angle ZMT$.

The circle $\omega$ constructed on the lateral side $AB$ of an isosceles triangle $ABC$ as diameter meets the lateral side $BC$ again at a point $D$. Prove that the perpendicular bisector of the segment $CD$ is tangent to the circle $\omega$.

Positive numbers $a_1$, $a_2$, $\ldots$, $a_{100}$ are such that $$a_1\cdot(a_2^2+1)=a_2\cdot(a_3^2+1)=a_3\cdot(a_4^2+1)=\ldots=a_{100}\cdot(a_1^2+1).$$ What is the largest possible number of distinct numbers among them?

$n$ children sit at a round table, and on the table there is a box full of "Belochka" sweets. First each of the children takes from the box at least one and at most $n$ sweets. After that each child keeps one of his sweets and gives the other sweets taken from the box, one each, to the children following him clockwise. In how many ways can the children take sweets so that in the end all have equally many sweets? (Two ways are considered different if at least one child takes a different number of sweets in these ways.)

Let $a$ and $b>1$ be natural numbers with $a+b=2029$. From the number $100\cdot 2026^2$ its remainder upon division by $a$ is subtracted; from the number obtained its remainder upon division by $b$ is subtracted; from the result its remainder upon division by $2026$ is subtracted. Then again the remainder upon division by $a$ is subtracted, and so on cyclically. After what smallest number of subtractions could the number $0$ be obtained?

A frog coloured the points of the number line in two colours. A grasshopper, having seen the colouring, wrote a rational number $a>0$ on a piece of paper, put it in an envelope and gave it to the frog. The frog turned away, and the grasshopper began to jump along the number line starting from the point $0$: $$0\to a\to 2a\to 3a\to 4a\to\ldots$$ After each jump the grasshopper tells the frog the colour of the point where he landed. Could the frog have devised a colouring such that at some moment she would be able to guess the number $a$ (and make sure she is right by opening the envelope)?

A circle with centre $I$ is inscribed in a triangle $ABC$ and touches its side $BC$ at a point $A_1$. The excircle of the triangle $ABC$ with centre $J$ touches the side $BC$ at a point $A_2$. The circumscribed circles of the triangles $AIA_1$ and $AJA_2$ meet the circumscribed circle of the triangle $ABC$ again at points $X$ and $Y$. Prove that $BC\parallel XY$.

Elves, dwarves and hobbits live in Middle-earth. There are $a_1$ ways to choose an elf and a dwarf acquainted with each other, $a_2$ ways to choose an acquainted elf and hobbit, and $a_3$ ways to choose an acquainted dwarf and hobbit. Prove that the number of ways to choose an elf, a dwarf and a hobbit pairwise acquainted with each other does not exceed $\sqrt{a_1a_2a_3}$.
